prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "HARMONY GOLD MINING CO LTD" (ticker HMY). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
   "nash": Tom Nash: the 12-step research process (“How to Find the Best Stocks in the Market” (Tom Nash, 2026))
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Harmony is a poor fit for Rule Breaker investing: it is a 75-year-old South African gold miner in a mature commodity industry, with no top-dog position in an emerging field, no brand advantage and no visionary founder. The stock has also lagged, trading at US$17.12 in October 2026 against a 52-week high of US$26.06.
summaries.buffett: Buffett's tenets favour durable moats and predictable earnings, and Harmony offers neither: it is a price taker whose results swung from a R1,052m loss in FY2022 to R29,349m of basic earnings in FY2026 on the gold price. The balance sheet is sound (net debt only R852m) and the price is low at about 6 times FY2026 earnings, but the business is not one he would typically own for decades.
summaries.munger: Munger warned against commodity businesses without pricing power, and Harmony's profits depend on the gold price, the rand and the safety of ultra-deep mines, so inverting the question turns up many ways things could go wrong. Its deep-level mining know-how is real but does not amount to a wonderful business at a fair price.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would classify Harmony as a cyclical, where buying at a low P/E near a cycle peak is a classic trap; its P/E of about 6 on record FY2026 earnings reflects a received gold price of US$3,811/oz. The story is simple (gold output of about 1.4Moz plus a new copper business) but depends on commodity prices rather than company-specific growth.
summaries.fisher: Fisher looked for companies with products that keep growing sales through research and superior selling, which a gold miner cannot offer. Management is experienced and moving into copper (CSA mine, Eva Copper), but there is no R&D engine and gold output is guided down to 1.30-1.40Moz in FY2027.
summaries.graham: On Graham's defensive criteria Harmony is large and cheap (about 6 times FY2026 earnings and about 10 times its three-year average) but fails on stability: it lost money in FY2020 and FY2022 and paid no dividend in FY2020. It would suit Graham's more enterprising approach better than the defensive checklist.
summaries.thiel: Harmony fails most of Thiel's seven questions: it has no proprietary technology, sells an undifferentiated commodity, does not have a monopoly, and has no secret others miss. Its durability rests on long-life reserves (27.4Moz attributable gold at June 2026) rather than a unique product.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner's focus on durable growth, operating discipline and a large secular opportunity fits only partly: Harmony has cut net debt quickly after the US$1.01bn MAC Copper purchase and generated R17,148m of adjusted free cash flow in FY2026, but its growth is driven by commodity prices rather than a technology shift.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller trades macro themes, and Harmony is a high-beta way to express a view on gold and the rand: FY2026 revenue rose 34% almost entirely because the received gold price rose 35%. It fits as a tactical macro position, not as a long-term compounder.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids cyclical, capital-intensive businesses with low and volatile returns, and Harmony's gross margin has ranged from 1.7% (FY2022) to 32.8% (FY2025) with capex of R17,106m in FY2026. It does not meet his 'buy good companies' test.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Harmony screens well right now: earnings yield is high (P/E about 6, group production profit of about US$2.96bn against an enterprise value near US$11bn) and recent return on capital is strong. The catch is that those numbers sit at a gold-price peak and can reverse sharply.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, great managers and great reinvestment opportunities; Harmony's business is a commodity producer without a moat, management is competent but not exceptional, and reinvestment in copper projects like Eva (US$1.55-1.75bn) is still unproven.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks low-risk, high-uncertainty bets in simple businesses; Harmony is simple and cheap on current earnings, but a falling gold price or a mining accident could cause permanent loss, so the downside is not tightly limited.
summaries.wood: Harmony has nothing to do with ARK's innovation platforms (AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain, multiomics); at most its copper output feeds electrification indirectly. It does not fit Cathie Wood's framework.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with high barriers to entry and little exposure to commodity prices; Harmony is fully exposed to gold and copper prices, so it fails his central criteria despite strong current cash flow.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep looked for businesses that share scale economies with customers to build ever-stronger positions; a gold miner sells at market prices and its mines deplete, so there is no scale-economics-shared flywheel.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed companies attacking huge, painful problems with new technology; Harmony is a mature mining company in an old industry and does not match what Sequoia looked for.
summaries.nash: Tom Nash explicitly avoids commodity producers, which rules Harmony out at the start despite strong FY2026 figures (revenue up 34%, adjusted free cash flow margin about 17%). It also carries slightly more debt than cash after the MAC Copper acquisition, an instant kill on his checklist.

momentum.evidence: HMY closed at US$17.12 on 16 October 2026, well below its 52-week high of US$26.06, with market value down about 10.5% over the year.

g4.evidence: CEO Beyers Nel is an experienced mining engineer and Newmont is Harmony's 50/50 partner in Wafi-Golpu, but there are no celebrated investors backing the company.

g6.evidence: At about 6 times FY2026 earnings (278 US cents EPS) the stock is generally seen as cheap rather than overvalued.

simple.evidence: The business is easy to understand: it mines about 1.4Moz of gold a year plus copper and sells it at market prices.

b2.evidence: Results are volatile: a loss attributable of R1,052m in FY2022 and R878m in FY2020, then a profit of R29,349m in FY2026.

integrity.evidence: Management ties dividends to free cash flow and paid a record R8.1bn for FY2026, but the FY2026 results restated prior-period figures to correct errors (note 25).

b6.evidence: The US$1.01bn MAC Copper purchase and Eva Copper build follow the industry-wide pivot to copper, though the CEO says he will not 'add ounces that reduce portfolio quality'.

roic.evidence: Return on average equity was about 32% in FY2025 (R14,384m profit) with little debt, but returns were negative in FY2022, so they are not consistent.

fcf.evidence: Adjusted free cash flow of R17,148m in FY2026 was about 58% of R29,349m basic earnings, held back by R17,106m of capex.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings rose from R2,238m (June 2024) to R14,584m (June 2025), but much is being reinvested in copper projects whose returns are not yet proven.

safety.evidence: At about 6 times FY2026 earnings the stock looks cheap, but value depends heavily on gold staying near US$4,000/oz, so a conservative valuation would be much lower.

fairprice.evidence: A P/E of about 6 and a forward P/E of about 5.4 on FY2027 consensus EPS of R52.41 is undemanding even for a cyclical miner.

mu5.evidence: It could be hurt by a falling gold price, a strong rand, power-cost increases, seismic accidents in ultra-deep mines, labour strikes or permitting delays in Papua New Guinea and Australia.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest in copper (Eva Copper at US$1.55-1.75bn, CSA expansion, 50% of Wafi-Golpu), but returns depend on copper prices and approvals.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear cyclical: earnings track the gold price, as FY2026 headline earnings jumped 87% on a 35% higher received price.

ly3.evidence: The P/E of about 6 is below FY2026 EPS growth of 103% and below consensus FY2027 EPS growth of about 22%.

runway.evidence: Gold output is guided down to 1.30-1.40Moz for FY2027, while copper should rise from 18,207t in FY2026 to 28,000-30,000t in FY2027 and more once Eva starts around end-2028.

ly7.evidence: The diluted share count crept up from 614.6m in FY2022 to 628.7m in FY2025, and there is no evidence of significant insider buying.

ly8.evidence: Only a handful of analysts (3 polled by S&P Global, 6 in revenue consensus) cover the US-listed shares of this South African miner.

fi2.evidence: Management is replacing ageing gold mines with new projects (Eva Copper, CSA) and life extensions such as Tshepong North to 15 years.

fi3.evidence: Harmony has no research and development programme in the usual sense; its exploration spending (R915m in FY2025) is aimed at extending mine lives.

fi4.evidence: It sells a commodity at market prices, so selling skill is not a differentiator.

longterm.evidence: Management is investing in long-life copper assets and a 10-year production profile, but also hedges production to protect near-term cash flows (R9,649m hedge loss in FY2026).

gr1.evidence: Harmony had FY2026 revenue of R99,238m (US$5,876m) and a market value of about US$10.9bn.

ni10.evidence: It reported losses attributable to owners in FY2020 (R878m) and FY2022 (R1,052m).

gr4.evidence: Harmony declared no dividend for FY2020, so it lacks a 20-year unbroken record.

eps10.evidence: Basic EPS rose from 842 SA cents in FY2021 to 4,701 SA cents in FY2026, far more than a one-third gain.

gr6.evidence: At R284.91 on the JSE the shares trade at about 10 times average basic EPS of the last three years (R13.86, R23.13 and R47.01).

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 6 times price/book of about 3.7 on June 2025 equity (R48,235m) gives about 22, near the 22.5 limit; June 2026 book value was higher but could not be confirmed.

th1.evidence: It uses standard deep-level mining and processing methods with no proprietary technology.

timing.evidence: Gold near US$4,165/oz and copper above US$5/lb make this a strong period for producers, but that is commodity timing rather than technology timing.

th3.evidence: It holds a small share of global gold output (about 1.4Moz of roughly 116Moz) rather than dominating a small market.

team.evidence: The leadership team is experienced (CEO Beyers Nel joined in 2003 and was Group COO), but it is not a world-class founder-led team.

th5.evidence: It needs no special distribution: gold refiners and copper smelters buy all it produces.

durable.evidence: Attributable reserves of 27.4Moz gold and 4.0Mt copper support decades of production, but individual mines deplete and costs are rising.

th7.evidence: Its strategy of buying unwanted South African mines and adding copper is followed by many peers.

trend.evidence: Its copper growth benefits from electrification and its gold from central-bank buying, but it is not a leading beneficiary of a platform shift.

dr1.evidence: HEPS rose 87% in FY2026 and consensus expects about 22% EPS growth in FY2027, but that is slower and depends on gold prices.

dr2.evidence: Copper output should rise to 28,000-30,000t in FY2027, but gold output is guided lower and Eva Copper only starts around end-2028.

dr4.evidence: Lower real interest rates and central-bank gold buying support the gold price, but a stronger rand (R16.48/US$ in October 2026 vs R16.89 average in FY2026) hurts rand margins.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include federal environmental approval for Eva Copper, Wafi-Golpu permitting, CSA ramp-up and any further rise in gold or copper prices.

dr7.evidence: As a single-commodity, single-country-heavy miner with operational risks, it is hard to justify as a large, concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin reached 32.8% in FY2025 but was only 1.7% in FY2022, showing it reflects gold prices rather than pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: FY2026 adjusted free cash flow of US$1,015m is about a 9% yield on a market value of about US$10.9bn.

gb2.evidence: FY2026 group production profit of about US$2.96bn (gold US$2,853m plus copper US$111m) is roughly a quarter of an enterprise value near US$11bn.

pa2.evidence: The shares are about a third below their 52-week high as costs rise and gold eased, but there is no clear one-off setback to fix.

pa4.evidence: Low debt (net debt R852m) limits financial risk, but a lasting fall in the gold price could permanently reduce value.

wo1.evidence: Harmony is a gold and copper miner with no role in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics.

wo2.evidence: Unit costs are rising, not falling: AISC rose 13% to R1,191,698/kg in FY2026.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine any innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its market is the global gold and copper market, which will not be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Earnings depend directly on gold and copper prices and the rand/dollar exchange rate.

ns1.evidence: It sells at market prices and does not pass scale savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: Copper growth (CSA, Eva, Wafi-Golpu) could strengthen it, but its South African gold mines are ageing and getting deeper.

va2.evidence: Copper supply for electrification addresses a real shortage, but gold mostly meets investment and jewellery demand.

tn1.evidence: It is a traditional gold miner retrofitting into copper, not a company built for a secular trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees a South African gold miner, while it is becoming a gold-copper producer with growing Australian assets (CSA and Eva Copper).

tn3.evidence: It is a commodity producer, one of the zones Nash avoids.

tn4.evidence: Revenue has grown five years running and it is profitable, though borrowings (about R9,476m) slightly exceed cash (R8,624m) after the MAC Copper deal.

tn5.evidence: Borrowings exceeded cash at 31 December 2025 (R12,894m vs R7,350m) and at 30 June 2026 (net debt R852m).

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 34% in FY2026 and about 26% a year over three years, but consensus expects only about 8% in FY2027.

tn7.evidence: FY2026 revenue growth of 34% plus an adjusted free cash flow margin of about 17% gives about 51.

tn8.evidence: Gold production profit rose 59% to R48,184m while revenue rose 34%, so costs grew more slowly than revenue.

tn9.evidence: It carries slightly more debt than cash (net debt R852m at June 2026), which is an instant kill on Nash's list.

tn10.evidence: It faces South African mining-charter and royalty rules, delayed federal environmental approvals for Eva Copper and permitting for Wafi-Golpu in Papua New Guinea.

tn11.evidence: It provides gold and copper that help refiners, investors and industry meet demand and charges market prices, but there is no reason to choose it over other producers.

tn13.evidence: Total about 70: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 10, operating margin 10, short interest 10, institutional ownership 5, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return 10, moat 0, CEO 5, pricing power 0, secular trend 5, culture 0, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year, but operating margin fell to -1.8% in FY2022 and net debt replaced net cash in FY2026.

tn15.evidence: At June 2025 total assets of R77,503m were about 2.7 times liabilities of R28,991m, the current ratio was 1.7 and liabilities were 0.6 times equity, and FY2026 production profit dwarfs finance costs of R1,663m.

tn18.evidence: Beyers Nel has been CEO only since January 2025 and there is no record of large open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: Harmony reports half-yearly and there is no reliable record of beats against consensus EPS.

tn21.evidence: The FY2026 results restated prior-period figures for errors (note 25), a red flag, though there is no acquisition spree, co-CEO or auditor issue.

tn22.evidence: It has large revenue (R99,238m), profits and dividends and does not rely on share sales or hype.

tn24.evidence: At about 6 times earnings the price implies falling profits, while revenue grew 34% in FY2026.

tn25.evidence: Using roughly 15% trimmed growth, a 17% FCF margin, 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate gives a value of roughly R330bn, well above the about R178bn market value, but this hinges on the gold price.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of about 5.4 on FY2027 consensus EPS of R52.41 with about 22% EPS growth gives a PEG near 0.25, below peers.
